title: Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a drug or small portfolio of drugs that safely produces meaningful clinical benefit against serious infections caused by several biologically distinct viral families. Its defining feature is useful treatment breadth across unrelated viruses, rather than activity against only one infection or closely related group. It does not require a single medicine that treats every virus. This is the proposed concept, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: breadth could reside in an individual drug or emerge collectively from a complementary portfolio. Those are different accomplishments and should be reported separately: a portfolio covering several families does not establish that each component has cross-family activity. Laboratory suppression of multiple viruses would be an intermediate result; the intended innovation requires benefit in patients at tolerable doses.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: a clinically effective portfolio spanning unrelated viral families could expand treatment options across several serious infections and reduce dependence on developing a separate medicine for each pathogen. The revolutionary feature would be the combination of breadth, safety and clinical usefulness. Broad laboratory activity alone would not deliver that change.

Such treatments could potentially be used before a precise diagnosis, but only where their demonstrated coverage includes the plausible causes of illness and prescribing criteria identify appropriate patients. Breadth would not eliminate the need for diagnosis: identifying the pathogen and assessing treatability could still determine whether a drug is suitable, which portfolio component to use and whether another treatment is needed.

A pre-existing portfolio could also provide an early treatment option during some new outbreaks. That possibility depends on the emerging virus being susceptible, an effective dosing regimen being established, acceptable safety in the affected population and sufficient availability. Activity against previously tested members of a family does not guarantee activity against every newly emerging member. Affordability, production and distribution are additional requirements; accessibility does not follow automatically from antiviral breadth.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed technical challenge: achieve a sufficiently shared vulnerability across unrelated viruses while preserving a useful margin between antiviral activity and harm to the patient. The research identifies viral diversity and dependence on host cells as central barriers: differences in replication machinery complicate shared targeting, while interference with cellular functions can introduce toxicity. These are coherent development challenges, but their scientific basis is not documented by the accessible content retained in the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: the breakthrough must bridge laboratory activity and clinical benefit. A candidate would need to work at exposures that patients can tolerate and under the conditions in which serious infections are actually treated. Its useful spectrum must also remain sufficiently dependable despite viral evolution. For a portfolio, complementary coverage must be established explicitly rather than inferred from a collection of promising individual results.

The remaining engineering and clinical task is therefore to establish which infections are treatable, at what doses, in which patients and with what resistance risks. Neither a shared biological target nor activity across a finite laboratory panel would by itself resolve those questions. The supplied material does not identify a demonstrated mechanism or candidate portfolio that has overcome these barriers.

current_state.text: The research states that existing antivirals have transformed treatment for several specific infections while effective therapies remain unavailable for many others. Those background claims remain unverified within this supplied evidence package. No assessable trial results, approved-drug inventory, quantitative efficacy findings or cross-family treatment demonstrations are included, so the package cannot establish the present extent of either antiviral success or the remaining treatment gap.

The supplied bibliographic record identifies a review attributed to Thibaut et al., titled “Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses,” with a stated publication date of 7 October 2026 and DOI 10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1. According to the supplied review, however, the retained HTML contains only a cookie-access message. The article identity, authors, publication date, abstract and substantive contents could not be verified from that artifact. The earlier description of access as a review abstract must therefore be corrected.

The source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026 and a saved extraction of 153 characters. Although its mechanical fields mark the artifact as verified and not truncated and list no extraction issues, the supplied review establishes that the retained text provides no identifiable article content. Successful saving of an access page does not establish access to the intended scientific document. The review also reports an empty bounded search record, so freshness of the treatment landscape cannot be assessed.

Consequently, the supplied material establishes neither a clinically validated cross-family portfolio nor a universal antiviral. This is a limit on the available evidence, not evidence that such results are false or that the concept is infeasible. Even if the listed review’s identity were confirmed, its stated focus on direct-acting agents against RNA viruses would require care when relating its conclusions to the broader concept of treatment across unrelated viral infections.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized clinical trials should show clinically meaningful benefit and acceptable safety for the same drug or a clearly defined small portfolio against serious infections from multiple biologically distinct viral families. Trial protocols should specify the patient populations, treatment timing, comparator, clinical outcomes and magnitude of benefit considered meaningful. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards; the supplied material supports no particular numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Meaningful clinical benefit and acceptable safety across distinct viral families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth assessment: the evidence should identify every tested virus and family, explain their biological diversity and distinguish the spectrum of each drug from the combined spectrum of the portfolio. Reproducible findings across independent studies and relevant patient populations would strengthen confidence. A finite set of successful tests establishes demonstrated breadth within that set, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reported tested-virus breadth distinguishes individual drugs from the portfolio

completion_criteria.text: Proposed prospective assessment: testing against newly emerging members should map susceptibility, effective dosing and resistance risks, including failures and uncertain results. Laboratory susceptibility could justify further investigation but would not automatically establish clinical effectiveness for a new outbreak. Follow-up should determine whether resistance or other changes materially narrow the usable spectrum.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective testing maps emerging-virus susceptibility, dosing and resistance risks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: a convincing demonstration should make clear where treatment is suitable and where evidence is absent, including safety restrictions and conditions for use before precise diagnosis. Claims of outbreak readiness should additionally establish availability and deployability. Claims of accessibility should be supported separately by evidence about cost, supply and delivery rather than inferred from pharmacological performance.
completion_criteria.label: Reported treatment boundaries identify suitable uses and evidence gaps

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: INF-05, near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections, is a direct complement. Better diagnosis could guide selection from an antiviral portfolio and identify infections outside its coverage. INF-07 could potentially support treatment while diagnostic results are pending, but its success would not complete the diagnostic objective.

INF-08, a pre-emptive vaccine against diverse pandemic coronaviruses, and INF-09, a rapid end-to-end vaccine response to a newly identified pathogen, share the outbreak-preparedness goal. Their central intervention is vaccination, whereas INF-07 concerns treatment of infection. Cross-family antiviral coverage is also a different breadth requirement from protection across diverse coronaviruses. INF-01, a broadly protective HIV vaccine, likewise pursues prevention rather than the treatment capability defined here.

INF-02, a safe scalable cure for established HIV infection, and INF-11, a treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B, overlap through antiviral treatment but demand distinct cure outcomes. A medicine could improve illness or suppress viral activity without producing a durable treatment-free cure. Conversely, a cure for one infection would not establish efficacy across unrelated viral families.

INF-10, prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus, and INF-14, mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes, concern consequences associated with viral infection. Effective acute antiviral treatment might become relevant to those objectives, but that is a conditional possibility requiring separate evidence. Benefit against an acute infection would not by itself establish prevention of multiple sclerosis or a post-viral syndrome.

INF-06, a dependable platform for generating new antibacterial treatments, and INF-15, a rapidly adaptable clinical phage-therapy platform, share drug-development and adaptable-treatment concerns but address bacterial infections. INF-03 and INF-12 address tuberculosis vaccination and curative treatment; INF-04 and INF-13 address malaria vector control and vaccination. Their prevention, transmission and treatment goals belong to the same infectious-disease portfolio, but success in INF-07 would not establish coverage of these nonviral infections or complete their separate objectives.

change_log.change: Preserved INF-07’s identity as clinically useful treatment across unrelated viral families, achievable by one drug or a small portfolio.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite the evidence-access failure and does not require a universal antiviral.

change_log.change: Corrected the claimed abstract access to an artifact containing only a cookie-access message; treated the article metadata as supplied but unverified.
change_log.reason: The validated review found no identifiable article content from which to verify the abstract, bibliographic identity or substantive coverage.

change_log.reason: The evidence gap neither supports those background claims nor disproves them.

change_log.change: Integrated conditions governing early prescribing, outbreak use and accessibility into the significance discussion.
change_log.reason: Coverage, susceptibility, dosing, safety, prescribing criteria and availability are separate requirements for those downstream benefits.

change_log.change: Separated individual-drug breadth, collective portfolio coverage, laboratory activity and patient benefit.
change_log.reason: These represent different accomplishments and should not be treated as interchangeable evidence of completion.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to address prespecified clinical benefit, biological diversity, reproducibility, prospective testing and practical limits.
change_log.reason: The review requested clearer operational criteria while cautioning that proposed thresholds are not consensus standards and finite tests cannot establish universality.

change_log.reason: Related objectives should remain distinct even where their tools or intended benefits overlap.

unresolved_issues: The listed review’s bibliographic identity, publication date, abstract and substantive contents remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The supplied evidence does not establish the current inventory of effective antivirals, the extent of unmet treatment needs or any demonstrated clinically effective cross-family portfolio.
The empty bounded search record prevents assessment of landscape freshness; the artifact’s retrieval date does not resolve that limitation.
The intended portfolio size, target infections and families, and allocation of breadth among individual drugs remain unspecified.
Clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, acceptable safety boundaries and the required biological diversity of demonstrations remain to be defined for particular indications.
Prospective susceptibility, resistance, prediagnostic prescribing and practical access requirements remain to be established.
The relationship between the listed review’s stated RNA-virus scope and the broader viral-treatment concept cannot be assessed without its scientific content.

brief.title: Medicines for unrelated viral infections
possible: People with serious viral infections could receive a medicine, or one of a small set, that works against several unrelated groups of viruses. Doctors could also have an early treatment option during some new outbreaks.
why: Patients would gain treatment options across several serious infections. A small set of medicines with complementary coverage could reduce the need to develop a separate treatment for each virus.

sources.showed: Their review describes medicines that act directly on viruses and the biological factors that determine which viruses they can treat.
sources.cited_for: It explains the case for a complementary set of medicines with broader coverage.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate safe, effective treatment across unrelated viral groups.

sources.showed: Patients receiving remdesivir recovered faster from Covid-19 than those receiving a placebo, a treatment without the active drug.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates a patient benefit from an antiviral medicine.
sources.not_established: Benefit against Covid-19 does not establish benefit against unrelated viral infections.

sources.showed: Zotatifin suppressed viruses from five families, biologically distinct groups, in laboratory cells.
sources.quote: Zotatifin also effectively inhibited multiple arboviruses (Chikungunya, Una, and Zika viruses), influenza A virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and vaccinia virus.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates that an individual compound can suppress unrelated viruses in cells.
sources.not_established: Cell experiments do not establish effective treatment at doses patients can tolerate.

sources.showed: In a preprint, the experimental compound cAIMP protected mice against chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Other cell experiments found that tested drugs differed in which viruses they inhibited.
sources.quote: In addition, cAIMP provided protection against CHIKV in a CHIKV-arthritis mouse model.
sources.cited_for: It supports animal testing and explicit mapping of each drug's coverage and failures.
sources.not_established: Protection in mice and activity in cells do not establish safe treatment across unrelated infections in patients.

shown: Beigel and colleagues demonstrated faster recovery with remdesivir in patients with Covid-19. Valdés-Torres and colleagues demonstrated broader activity with zotatifin in laboratory cells. These are separate steps toward combining patient benefit with coverage across unrelated viruses.
missing: Trials still need to demonstrate meaningful benefit and acceptable safety across unrelated infections for the same medicine or a defined small set.
Each medicine's coverage, effective doses and risk of viruses evolving to evade treatment need to be established.
Suitable patients, rules for treatment before diagnosis, and practical outbreak supply and delivery need to be established.

milestones.label: Safe patient benefit across unrelated viral groups
milestones.explanation: Trials with randomly assigned treatments would have to show meaningful benefit and acceptable safety across unrelated infections for the same drug or defined small set. This would establish useful treatment breadth.

milestones.label: Clear coverage for each medicine and the whole set
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to identify each virus and distinguish each drug's coverage from the combined coverage. This would establish how broadly each treatment works without implying it treats every virus.

milestones.label: Emerging viruses tested for treatment response
milestones.explanation: Testing as new viruses emerge would have to map whether treatment works, effective doses and risks of viruses evolving to evade it. This would reveal whether usable coverage holds up as viruses change.

milestones.label: Clear treatment boundaries and conditions for use
milestones.explanation: Results would have to define suitable uses, safety limits, gaps and rules for treatment before diagnosis. Outbreak readiness would also require availability and delivery; access claims would require evidence on cost and supply.

uncertain: The size of the medicine set, target infections and division of coverage among drugs remain undefined.
What counts as meaningful benefit, acceptable safety and sufficiently unrelated viral groups must be decided for particular uses.
Activity against known viruses may not predict treatment success against newly emerging relatives.

page.title: Cross-family antivirals for respiratory infections
page.definition: A single antiviral has approved treatment indications for influenza and a respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family, a taxonomic group of related viruses.

goal.need: Seasonal influenza causes 3–5 million severe illnesses annually. FDA states that currently approved influenza antivirals are not expected to benefit COVID-19. BARDA seeks a therapeutic covering influenza and other respiratory viruses.

figures.caption: Estimated annual global burden of seasonal influenza

statements.context: A recommendation to G7 governments in the academies' statement on antiviral preparedness.

statements.quote: All should be ready for Phase 2 trials against a new virus, with testing protocols in place, and be ready for manufacture.
statements.context: The passage concerns panels containing virus-specific and broad-spectrum antivirals. The meeting note records participants' views and is not government policy.

completion.title: FDA approves one antiviral for influenza and a respiratory virus from another family.
completion.criterion: The same antiviral receives FDA marketing approval for influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family, with a novel mechanism of action for influenza. BARDA's clinical target is clinically meaningful faster symptom alleviation versus untreated patients when treatment begins within 48 hours of symptom onset. Each claimed infection must be covered by the approved indications.
completion.set_by: BARDA Influenza & Emerging Infectious Diseases Division, respiratory broad-spectrum antiviral target product profile: Goal 1, multiple-family objective, and Indication for Use and Clinical Efficacy table rows; FDA determines marketing approval.
completion.threshold_quote: an FDA-approved broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutic that has a novel mechanism of action for influenza and other viral respiratory diseases.
completion.basis: BARDA pairs a multiple-family objective with an indication threshold of influenza plus at least one other respiratory virus. The different-family interpretation preserves the cross-family scope distinguished by Thibaut and colleagues. FDA approval determines clinical use; BARDA's profile is an aspirational planning tool rather than regulatory guidance.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral inhibits viruses from more than one family in cells.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate antiviral activity in cells (BARDA component 3B); the cross-family scope follows BARDA's multiple-family objective. A study published on 19 March 2026 found zotatifin activity against viruses from five families. At 50 nM, it reduced Mayaro virus titres by more than 4 log10 in three independent experiments performed in triplicate. This establishes laboratory breadth, without establishing clinical respiratory indications.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, component 3B; multiple-family scope from its respiratory antiviral target product profile. Component 3B is stated in the table.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral demonstrates animal efficacy and undergoes initial toxicity and exposure studies.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate animal efficacy at the intended dose, schedule, duration and route, with initial toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies (BARDA 4A–4B). A study published on 2 December 2021 found that oral 4′-fluorouridine reduced RSV lung virus in mice (5 mg/kg daily, started 24 hours after infection; n=5/group) and SARS-CoV-2 shedding in ferrets (20 mg/kg daily, started 12 hours after infection; n=3–4/group). These findings establish the efficacy component across two respiratory virus families.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, components 4A and 4B. The criteria are stated in the table.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral completes Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic assessment in people.
milestones.criterion: After an investigational new drug application is allowed to proceed, complete initial human safety and pharmacokinetic assessment (BARDA 6B–6C). A PROPEL conference poster reported 36 adults with COVID-19: 27 received zotatifin, at 0.01–0.035 mg/kg, and nine received placebo. Preliminary data as of 6 February 2023 included no serious adverse events and one grade 3 creatine phosphokinase elevation. The conference result was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, components 6B and 6C; FDA's investigational new drug process governs permission to begin human trials. The BARDA criteria are stated in the table.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral completes Phase 2 trials assessing safety and efficacy in infected people.
milestones.criterion: Complete expanded Phase 2 clinical safety trials (BARDA 7B), assessing efficacy and adverse effects according to the protocol. A Phase 2b/3 nitazoxanide trial enrolled 624 people aged 12–65 years between 27 December 2010 and 30 April 2011. In participants with confirmed influenza, 600 mg twice daily for five days yielded median symptom duration of 95.5 hours versus 116.7 hours with placebo (P=0.0084). This result concerns influenza alone.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, component 7B; FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, Phase 2 purpose. Component 7B is stated in the table.

milestones.title: Pivotal trials establish an antiviral's clinical benefit for both respiratory indications.
milestones.criterion: Pivotal trials establish treatment benefit and characterise safety for the claimed indications. BARDA targets faster symptom alleviation when treatment starts within 48 hours. ACTT-1, published on 8 October 2020, found median COVID-19 recovery of 10 versus 15 days among 1,062 randomized adults. Nitazoxanide's Phase 3 influenza trial ended on 16 April 2015: 1,941 participants; primary monotherapy comparison, 185 versus 180 patients, 119.1 versus 116.5 hours (P=0.8622). These results do not establish the combined indications.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, Phase 3 treatment-benefit criterion; BARDA respiratory antiviral target product profile, Clinical Efficacy table row.
milestones.threshold_quote: Researchers design Phase 3 studies to demonstrate whether or not a product offers a treatment benefit to a specific population.

milestones.title: A marketing application seeks approval of one antiviral for both respiratory indications.
milestones.criterion: A New Drug Application or Biologics License Application for the same antiviral is submitted to FDA, covering influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family. BARDA component 8B recognises submission of this application after pivotal studies; component 8C separately recognises approval. The submission contains the evidence and proposed prescribing information supporting the claimed indications.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, component 8B, applied to the indication scope in its respiratory antiviral target product profile. The submission criterion is stated in the table.

not_found: No numerical minimum for clinically meaningful symptom shortening was found in BARDA's respiratory antiviral target product profile.
No fixed portfolio size or required family coverage was specified in the BARDA, G7 academy or UK documents.
No FDA approval or marketing application covering the specified influenza and other-family respiratory indications was located.
